questions.q: Which classic point on the right lower quadrant is maximally tender in acute appendicitis?
questions.hint: Located one-third of the way from the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) to the umbilicus.
questions.explanation: McBurney's point lies one-third of the distance from the right ASIS to the umbilicus and is classically tender in acute appendicitis.

questions.q: Which sign describes right lower quadrant pain elicited when palpating the left lower quadrant?
questions.hint: Referred pain to the right iliac fossa during left iliac fossa pressure.
questions.explanation: Rovsing's sign is positive when pressure in the left lower quadrant causes pain in the right lower quadrant.

questions.q: Which imaging modality is preferred first-line in a pregnant patient with suspected acute appendicitis?
options: A) Graded compression ultrasound or MRI without gadolinium
D) Diagnostic laparoscopy before any imaging
questions.hint: Avoid ionizing radiation when possible in pregnancy.
questions.explanation: Graded compression ultrasound (followed by non-contrast MRI if inconclusive) avoids ionizing radiation in pregnancy.

questions.q: A patient with perforated peptic ulcer presents with sudden severe epigastric pain and rigid abdomen. What finding is commonly seen on an erect chest radiograph?
options: A) Pneumoperitoneum (free air under the diaphragm)
D) Coin lesion in the right lower lobe
questions.hint: Look beneath the hemidiaphragms on an upright CXR.
questions.explanation: Perforated hollow viscus often demonstrates free intraperitoneal air (pneumoperitoneum) beneath the diaphragm on an erect chest X-ray.

questions.q: Which triad characterizes acute cholangitis (Charcot's triad)?
options: A) Fever, right upper quadrant pain, and jaundice
C) Ascites, spider nevi, and asterixis
D) Dysphagia, weight loss, and anemia
questions.hint: Infection of an obstructed biliary tree produces systemic infection + biliary signs.
questions.explanation: Charcot's triad consists of fever/rigors, right upper quadrant pain, and jaundice.

questions.q: Which blood pressure threshold at >= 20 weeks gestation with new proteinuria or end-organ dysfunction defines preeclampsia?
options: A) BP >= 140/90 mmHg on two occasions at least 4 hours apart
C) BP >= 125/80 mmHg in the first trimester only
D) BP < 130/85 mmHg with edema alone
questions.hint: Standard systolic/diastolic cutoff is 140/90 mmHg.
questions.explanation: Gestational hypertension and preeclampsia use a blood pressure threshold of >= 140/90 mmHg at or after 20 weeks of gestation.

questions.q: Which medication is first-line to prevent and treat eclamptic seizures?
questions.hint: Anticonvulsant of choice in severe preeclampsia and eclampsia.
questions.explanation: Magnesium sulfate is superior to phenytoin and diazepam for preventing and controlling eclamptic seizures.

questions.q: Which three laboratory abnormalities form the HELLP syndrome acronym?
options: A) Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets
B) Hypoglycemia, Elevated Lactate, Low Potassium
C) Hypercalcemia, Elevated Lipase, Low Phosphate
D) Hypoxia, Elevated Leukocytes, Low Sodium
questions.hint: Think RBC breakdown, transaminases, and thrombocytopenia.
questions.explanation: HELLP stands for Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, and Low Platelets.

questions.q: Which daily folic acid dose is recommended preconceptionally and in early pregnancy to reduce neural tube defects?
options: A) 0.4 mg (400 mcg) daily for standard risk
C) 20 mg daily for all women
D) Only started after 28 weeks gestation
questions.hint: Neural tube closure occurs early in the first month after conception.
questions.explanation: Standard daily folic acid supplementation is 400 mcg (0.4 mg) starting before conception through the first trimester.

questions.q: Which presentation classically distinguishes abruptio placentae from placenta previa?
options: A) Painful vaginal bleeding often with uterine tenderness/hypertonicity
B) Painless bright-red bleeding without uterine irritability
C) Absent fetal movement with painless watery discharge only
D) Bleeding strictly limited to the first 6 weeks
questions.hint: Placental separation vs low-lying placenta covering the os.
questions.explanation: Placental abruption typically presents with painful bleeding and a tender or rigid uterus, whereas placenta previa classically causes painless bleeding.

questions.q: Which hormone pattern is most typical of overt primary hypothyroidism?
options: A) High TSH and low Free T4
B) Low TSH and high Free T4
C) Low TSH and low Free T4
D) Normal TSH and high Free T3
questions.hint: Pituitary responds to low thyroid hormone by raising TSH.
questions.explanation: Primary hypothyroidism features low thyroid hormones (low Free T4) and elevated TSH due to loss of negative feedback.

questions.q: Which test is best for initial screening of acromegaly?
questions.hint: Reflects sustained growth hormone exposure better than a single random GH.
questions.explanation: Serum IGF-1 is the preferred initial screening test for suspected acromegaly.

questions.q: Which diagnostic cutoff for HbA1c supports a diagnosis of diabetes mellitus?
questions.hint: Prediabetes is typically 5.7%–6.4%.
questions.explanation: An HbA1c of 6.5% or higher (confirmed on repeat testing when asymptomatic) diagnoses diabetes mellitus.

questions.q: In DKA with serum potassium 3.0 mmol/L, what must happen before starting an insulin infusion?
options: A) Give IV fluids and potassium replacement first until K+ >= 3.3 mmol/L
B) Give an immediate high-dose insulin bolus without potassium
questions.hint: Insulin shifts potassium into cells and can worsen severe hypokalemia.
questions.explanation: Potassium must be repleted prior to insulin infusion when K+ < 3.3 mmol/L to prevent life-threatening arrhythmias.

questions.q: In suspected adrenal crisis, which immediate treatment should not be delayed for lab results?
options: A) IV hydrocortisone and rapid IV isotonic saline
questions.hint: Treat glucocorticoid deficiency and volume depletion immediately.
questions.explanation: Immediate IV/IM hydrocortisone and rapid isotonic saline resuscitation are essential in adrenal crisis.

questions.q: Which five components make up the Apgar score assessed at 1 and 5 minutes after birth?
options: A) Appearance (color), Pulse, Grimace (reflex irritability), Activity (tone), Respiration
B) Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure
C) Temperature, Weight, Length, Head circumference, Fontanelle
D) Heart rate, Blood glucose, Bilirubin, Oxygen sat, Hemoglobin
questions.hint: Each letter of A-P-G-A-R corresponds to a clinical sign scored 0, 1, or 2.
questions.explanation: The Apgar score evaluates Appearance, Pulse, Grimace, Activity, and Respiration at 1 and 5 minutes.

questions.q: Which vitamin is routinely administered shortly after birth to prevent hemorrhagic disease of the newborn?
questions.hint: Required for hepatic synthesis of clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X.
questions.explanation: Prophylactic vitamin K prevents vitamin K deficiency bleeding (hemorrhagic disease of the newborn).

questions.q: Which sign in a child with acute dehydration indicates severe dehydration?
options: A) Lethargy/unconsciousness, sunken eyes, very slow skin pinch (>2 sec), or unable to drink
B) Alert, drinking eagerly, normal skin pinch
C) Mild thirst only with normal pulse and tears
questions.hint: Look for severe neurological or perfusion/skin turgor signs.
questions.explanation: Severe dehydration is marked by lethargy/altered consciousness, sunken eyes, poor skin turgor, and inability to drink or drinking poorly.

questions.q: At approximately what age does a typically developing infant sit without support?
questions.hint: Gross motor milestone around the middle of the first year.
questions.explanation: Most infants sit unsupported around 6 months of age.

questions.q: Which immunization is typically given at birth in routine national schedules alongside OPV0 and HepB0?
questions.hint: Bacillus Calmette-Guerin.
questions.explanation: BCG is given at birth (or as soon as possible thereafter) in routine childhood immunization schedules.

questions.q: On a standard PA chest radiograph, which structure normally forms the right heart border?
questions.hint: The left ventricle forms most of the lower left heart border.
questions.explanation: The right heart border on a PA chest X-ray is formed primarily by the right atrium.

questions.q: Which CT modality is typically preferred to evaluate suspected acute renal colic / ureteric stones without IV contrast?
options: A) Non-contrast CT KUB (kidneys, ureters, bladder)
questions.hint: Most urinary calculi are radiopaque on unenhanced CT.
questions.explanation: Non-contrast CT of the kidneys, ureters, and bladder is highly sensitive and specific for detecting urinary tract calculi.

questions.q: Which plain abdominal X-ray sign suggests pneumoperitoneum when free air outlines both sides of the bowel wall?
questions.hint: Gas inside the lumen and gas outside the lumen make the wall visible on both sides.
questions.explanation: Rigler's sign occurs when free intraperitoneal air outlines the outer wall of a loop of bowel already containing intraluminal gas.

questions.q: In suspected acute ischemic stroke within the early window, which imaging test is rapidly performed first to rule out hemorrhage?
questions.hint: Acute blood appears bright (hyperdense) on non-contrast CT.
questions.explanation: Non-contrast CT of the head is the rapid first-line imaging test in acute stroke to exclude intracranial hemorrhage before thrombolysis.

questions.q: Which ultrasound feature typically helps differentiate a simple benign cyst from a solid mass?
options: A) Anechoic interior with posterior acoustic enhancement and thin smooth wall
B) Marked internal vascularity on Doppler with irregular spiculated margins
C) Shadowing gallstones inside a thickened wall
D) Absent fluid component and dense bone shadowing
questions.hint: Fluid transmits sound waves with less attenuation than surrounding tissue.
questions.explanation: A simple cyst on ultrasound is classically anechoic, has a thin smooth wall, and demonstrates posterior acoustic enhancement.

questions.q: Which fracture is classically described as a distal radius fracture with dorsal angulation ('dinner fork' deformity)?
questions.hint: Occurs typically after a fall onto an outstretched hand (FOOSH) with dorsal displacement.
questions.explanation: A Colles' fracture is a fracture of the distal radius with dorsal displacement/angulation of the distal fragment.

questions.q: Tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox after a fall on an outstretched hand raises suspicion for fracture of which carpal bone?
questions.hint: Blood supply enters distally, placing the proximal pole at risk of avascular necrosis.
questions.explanation: Anatomical snuffbox tenderness warrants evaluation for a scaphoid fracture, which carries risk of non-union and avascular necrosis.

questions.q: Which combination of findings is classic for acute compartment syndrome?
options: A) Severe pain out of proportion (especially with passive stretch), paresthesia, pallor, pulselessness, paralysis
B) Morning stiffness <30 minutes in DIP joints only
C) Chronic low back pain improving with exercise
D) painless clicking in the shoulder
questions.hint: Pain on passive stretch is an early warning sign before late pulselessness.
questions.explanation: Acute compartment syndrome presents with severe pain (especially on passive stretch) and neurovascular deficits requiring urgent fasciotomy.

questions.q: Which classification system is widely used for pediatric physeal (growth plate) fractures?
questions.hint: Grades I through V based on fracture involvement of the physis, metaphysis, and epiphysis.
questions.explanation: The Salter-Harris classification categorizes pediatric growth plate fractures (Types I–V) to guide management and prognosis.

questions.q: A displaced mid-shaft humerus fracture can injure which nerve, causing wrist drop?
questions.hint: Runs along the radial groove of the humerus and innervates wrist/finger extensors.
questions.explanation: The radial nerve courses along the spiral/radial groove of the humerus and is vulnerable in humeral shaft fractures, leading to wrist drop.
